chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: What 'studio musician' means; leaving Goodman for the studios and Lee Konitz
summary: Maxwell defends studio work as an ethical need to support a family; Lee Konitz asks him for studio dates.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well, I happen to know that you -- most of the music world and certainly in New York City, we know about how much you helped others, so many of us, young people as well as professional players. And I don't know whether you'd like to mention any of their names but first I'd like to ask
you to talk about this. What about the words, "studio musician"? How do you feel about that?

Well, it's kind of a put-down word. But studio musicians, it really is sort of a jack of all trades, but not necessarily master of none, because most of the studio musicians I know are the top players and many of them were the top jazz players. It was always a critical word.

Now, I know when I left Benny Goodman's band, I left it in 1943 and I went into the studios. I had a good friend, Gil Evans, who used to needle me all of the time about it. And he'd see me up the Union, collecting my checks, and he'd make corny remarks, "$1 million, $2 million," or something. And I always felt a little apologetic about it. But I had a family to support and I have children, and I didn't believe that I had the right to go out on the road and enjoy myself playing in jazz bands or whatever and leave my wife and kids at home. There's no point in having a wife and kids, you know. And I'm not saying people shouldn't do that, because if you have an alternative I think you're ethically obliged to do it. Besides the fact I like being with my wife and family.

And truthfully, I enjoyed studio work. But what sort of took the stigma off from it was within the first five years, I mention names, I guess it won't hurt; I went to hear Lee Konitz one night. At that time he was a big jazz player and everything. And he was talking to me and he said, you know,
man, just because I'm a jazz player, you know, I can read and spell. If there are any gigs you'd like to do, I'd appreciate it if you'd fix me up.
Now, I know that for a while Roy was doing that kind of work. He was doing the Mildred Bailey Show --

Yeah, Charlie Shavers was doing the Mildred Bailey Show. That's studio work. And they've done transcriptions of stuff. But of course, these men are big stylists and they don't have to do that work. But for the person who wasn't a famous jazz player, you know, like they were, I don't see, you know, that it hurt anybody.
Look at yourself. My, God, all the jazz bands you've played with and you did most of the studio work in New York, certainly most of the dates I went on you were on. And --

Yeah, Jimmy. I could go back a little further than that but right now I don't want to. Because I agree wholeheartedly with you that it has sort of a putdown name. Studio Musician. But the studio musician to me supplies all of the best musicians that came out of the big bands when the big bands were starting to disintegrate.
